title: AI Skills and Plugins Explained
description: Understand what skills and plugins are, how they differ from tools, and what they mean for everyday AI users.

data.text: The terminology around AI extensibility is confusing — skills, plugins, tools, and functions are often used interchangeably across different platforms. This lesson gives you a clear decoder so you understand what each term means in practice, and how these concepts make AI tools more powerful.

At its core, the concept is simple: a language model on its own can only generate text. To be genuinely useful — to search the web, read your files, send an email, query a database — it needs to be able to reach outside itself and trigger an action. That capability goes by different names on different platforms. Knowing what each name actually refers to cuts through the marketing noise and helps you understand what any AI tool can actually do.

data.caption: All these terms describe the same fundamental concept: giving an AI model a way to call an external capability. The vocabulary differs by platform.

data.text: These terms all describe the same fundamental concept: giving an AI model a way to call an external capability. The terminology varies by platform but the concept is identical.
How tool calling actually works under the hood

When an AI model has access to tools, it does not call them automatically. The model reads your message, decides whether a tool would help answer it, and if so, outputs a structured request — a tool call — specifying which tool to use and with what inputs. The host application (ChatGPT, Claude, your own code) intercepts that request, actually runs the tool, and feeds the result back into the model's context. The model then generates a final response using the tool's output.

data.caption: A tool call is a structured output from the model that the host application executes — the model itself never directly runs code or accesses the web.
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
  participant User
  participant Model
  participant Host as Host App
  participant Tool as External Tool

  User->>Model: "What is today's weather in London?"
  Model->>Host: Tool call: get_weather(city="London")
  Host->>Tool: Execute get_weather API
  Tool-->>Host: {temp: 14°C, condition: "cloudy"}
  Host-->>Model: Tool result: 14°C, cloudy
  Model->>User: "It's currently 14°C and cloudy in London."

data.text: This design matters for two reasons. First, it means the model is never directly executing code or hitting an API — the host application controls what actually happens, which is where safety guardrails are applied. Second, it means a model can use multiple tools in sequence, building up context across several calls before generating a final answer. That chaining of tools is what makes agentic behaviour possible.
Read tools vs. write tools: a critical distinction

Not all tools carry the same risk. A tool that reads information — searching the web, loading a file, fetching calendar events — is low risk: if something goes wrong, no state has changed. A tool that writes or acts — sending an email, deleting a file, posting to a system, making a purchase — is irreversible. The same AI action that feels like a helpful shortcut can cause real damage if it runs without a confirmation step.

Send email, submit a form, make an API call, execute a purchase

data.title: Agentic tools need human oversight
data.text: The more tools an AI has — especially write and action tools — the more important it is to understand what it can do without asking you first. Before enabling an AI assistant with broad permissions, ask: which of these actions are irreversible, and does it require confirmation before taking them?
What this means for you as a user
You are already using skills and tools any time you use AI with built-in capabilities. Here is how each concept maps to things you do every day:

data.text: MCP: the standard that is changing how tools work

Until recently, tool integrations were fragmented: each AI platform defined its own format for tools and plugins, and a tool built for ChatGPT would not work with Claude or any other model without being rewritten. MCP — the Model Context Protocol, introduced by Anthropic in 2024 — is an open standard that defines a common format for exposing tools to AI models. An MCP server packages a set of tools following this standard, and any AI application that supports MCP can use it immediately, regardless of which company built the AI.

Think of MCP the way you think of USB: before USB, every device needed its own proprietary connector. USB standardized the interface so that any device could connect to any computer. MCP does the same for AI tools — write it once, use it with any MCP-compatible AI. The practical effect for users is that the ecosystem of available tools is growing fast, and the same integrations will work across different AI products as MCP adoption spreads.

data.caption: MCP decouples tools from AI models — one MCP server works with any MCP-compatible AI host.

data.text: Tool calling in practice: what good looks like

data.title: Multi-tool workflow: research and draft
data.content:
You ask an AI assistant: "Find the three most recent papers on sleep and memory consolidation, then draft a two-paragraph summary for a general audience."

Behind the scenes:
1. web_search('sleep memory consolidation recent research') → returns results
2. fetch_page(url_1) → reads paper abstract
3. fetch_page(url_2) → reads paper abstract
4. fetch_page(url_3) → reads paper abstract
5. Model synthesises all retrieved content
6. Model generates the two-paragraph summary

You see only the final answer. The tool calls happened silently, each building context for the next step. This is a simple agentic loop — and it is how most AI assistants with web access work today.

data.title: Where it can go wrong: ambiguous tool permissions
data.content:
You ask a Copilot-style assistant: "Clear out my inbox."

If the assistant has write access to email with no confirmation step, it may archive, delete, or mark-as-read hundreds of emails before you can stop it. The tool call is technically correct — it did what you asked. The problem is that 'clear out my inbox' was ambiguous, the action was irreversible, and there was no human review step.

Best practice: before enabling AI write access to high-value systems (email, calendar, files), check whether the platform requires confirmation before destructive actions. If it does not, treat the tool as higher risk.

data.text: What to look for when evaluating AI tools

data.title: As an AI user, these are the questions that matter more than the terminology:
items: What tools does this AI have access to? (Search, code, files, APIs)
Can it take actions in the real world, or is it read-only?
What permissions does it need? (Principle of least privilege applies)
Is there a human review step before irreversible actions?
Does the platform support MCP? (More MCP compatibility = more future integrations)

data.text: The principle of least privilege for AI tools

Least privilege is a security principle from software engineering: any system should have only the minimum permissions it needs to do its job. It applies directly to AI tool access. An AI assistant that needs to read your calendar does not need write access to your email. An AI that summarises documents does not need access to your file system — only the specific document you share with it.

In practice, many AI platforms request broad permissions because it makes setup easier and covers more use cases. That convenience trades off against risk: broader permissions mean a single misunderstood instruction or a prompt injection attack can cause wider damage. When setting up AI tools with real-world access, apply least privilege deliberately: grant read-only access before write access, limit scope to specific folders or accounts rather than everything, and review what permissions are actually needed for the tasks you plan to use.

data.caption: Applying least privilege to AI tool access: start narrow, expand only when needed.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  Task[Define the task the AI needs to do]
  Task --> ReadOnly{Does it only need\nto READ data?}
  ReadOnly -->|Yes| GrantRead[Grant read-only access\nto the minimum needed]
  ReadOnly -->|No| WriteNeeded{Does it need\nto WRITE or ACT?}
  WriteNeeded -->|Yes| Confirm[Grant write access +\nrequire confirmation step]
  WriteNeeded -->|Destructive| HumanLoop[Require explicit\nhuman approval before execution]

  style GrantRead fill:#d1f3d8,stroke:#1a7f37,color:#1a7f37
  style Confirm fill:#fff8c5,stroke:#9a6700,color:#9a6700
  style HumanLoop fill:#ffebe9,stroke:#cf222e,color:#cf222e

data.title: Bottom line
points: Different words, same concept: giving AI access to external capabilities
Tools, skills, plugins, actions, MCP servers = all ways to give AI real-world access
Tool calls are structured outputs — the host app executes them, not the model directly
Read tools are low risk; write and action tools can be irreversible — require confirmation
MCP is the emerging standard that makes tools portable across AI platforms
As a user: focus on WHAT the tool can do, and whether it's safe
Apply least privilege: grant only the minimum permissions the task actually needs
The richer the tool ecosystem, the more useful the AI becomes as an agent
